scams.name: Hartsfield-Jackson (ATL) Airport Rideshare & Taxi Scams
scams.description:
ATL is the busiest airport in the Western Hemisphere by passenger count, processing more than 100 million passengers annually. International and first-time arrivals are the primary targets: unlicensed drivers and "black car" touts position themselves in the baggage claim area, before the regulated taxi and rideshare zones outside, and quote flat rates of $60–$120 for standard downtown runs.

The licensed metered taxi fare to downtown runs $30–$45; Uber and Lyft, booked through the app from the designated pickup zones (North Terminal: North Economy Parking; South Terminal: South Economy Parking), run $20–$35 depending on surge. Some Uber and Lyft drivers accept the on-app booking, then demand an additional cash "airport surcharge" or "mandatory tip" at drop-off. Fake "MARTA ticket agents" stationed inside the terminal try to sell overpriced transit passes.

The MARTA train eliminates every transport scam at once. Take the MARTA Red or Gold Line from ATL station to downtown Five Points for $2.50 in 20 minutes, and buy the Breeze Card at the official MARTA kiosk inside the station. If you prefer a rideshare, match the app pickup location before approaching any vehicle, and never engage drivers who solicit inside the terminal.
scams.avoidance: Take the MARTA Red or Gold Line from ATL to Five Points downtown: $2.50, 20 minutes. Use Uber or Lyft at the designated rideshare pickup (North or South Terminal Economy Parking). A licensed taxi with the meter running costs $30–$45 to downtown. Never engage drivers soliciting at baggage claim. Buy the Breeze Card at the official MARTA kiosk for $2.50.
scams.location: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) arrivals, North/South Terminal pickup zones, MARTA station
scams.tldr: At Hartsfield-Jackson (ATL), unlicensed drivers solicit arriving passengers at baggage claim with "flat $60" offers to downtown. The legitimate MARTA train to downtown Five Points is $2.50 and takes 20 minutes, while licensed taxis run $30–$45 on the meter and Uber and Lyft run $20–$35 from the designated pickup zones.

scams.name: Georgia Aquarium & Coca-Cola Museum Reseller Scams
scams.description:
The Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, and CNN Center are clustered at Pemberton Place near Centennial Olympic Park, Atlanta's primary tourist anchor. Google searches for "Atlanta Aquarium tickets" or "World of Coca-Cola tickets" return sponsored reseller links above the official sites, and touts position themselves at the park entrance to intercept families before they reach the venue ticket booths.

Reseller sites charge $75–$120 for Georgia Aquarium tickets sold at georgiaaquarium.org for $49.95; World of Coca-Cola tickets at more than $40 for what costs $22 direct at worldofcoca-cola.com; and "Atlanta CityPASS bundles" at more than $120 for what the legitimate citypass.com sells for $85–$95. The touts at Centennial Olympic Park charge more than $120 for the Aquarium and Coca-Cola combo that costs $72 bought directly at both official sites. Book the Georgia Aquarium at georgiaaquarium.org ($49.95), World of Coca-Cola at worldofcoca-cola.com ($22), and the Atlanta CityPASS only at citypass.com ($85–$95). Scroll past the sponsored Google results to the official domain, and reject touts at the park.
scams.avoidance: Book the Georgia Aquarium direct at georgiaaquarium.org: adult $49.95. Book World of Coca-Cola direct at worldofcoca-cola.com: adult $22. Buy the Atlanta CityPASS direct at citypass.com: $85–$95 for 5 attractions. Reject touts at Centennial Olympic Park. Avoid Google ads for "Atlanta tickets" and scroll past the sponsored results.
scams.location: Online — third-party reseller sites for Georgia Aquarium, World of Coca-Cola, CNN Center tickets; touts at Pemberton Place
scams.tldr: Third-party reseller sites list Georgia Aquarium tickets at $75–$120 per person, 50 to 150 percent above the direct price of $49.95 at georgiaaquarium.org, and touts at Centennial Olympic Park sell Aquarium plus World of Coca-Cola combos for more than $120 for attractions that cost $72 combined when booked direct.

scams.name: 'US Customs and Border Protection' Phone Scam
scams.description:
Hartsfield-Jackson is the primary international gateway for the Southeast, which gives the "CBP officer calling about your ATL package" script a specific geographic plausibility for anyone who recently transited or is planning to depart. The caller ID is spoofed to show a 404 Atlanta number, and the opening statement, "a package in your name has been seized at Hartsfield-Jackson," is designed to create immediate fear before the target can think critically about whether they are expecting any package.

The caller escalates by transferring to a "supervisor" who demands $1,000–$5,000 by Zelle, Venmo, gift cards, or wire transfer to "clear the warrant" and "avoid arrest at the airport on your departure." Taking time to verify or calling back is explicitly discouraged: "your window closes in 30 minutes." The payment method is the definitive tell. CBP has no mechanism to accept Zelle, gift cards, or cryptocurrency for any purpose.

This scam has exactly one correct response. Hang up immediately. US Customs and Border Protection never calls travelers demanding payment by phone, and all CBP communications about real issues arrive by USPS mail. If you are genuinely concerned, call the official CBP contact center at 1-877-CBP-5511, and report the scam to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
scams.avoidance: Hang up immediately: CBP never calls demanding payment by phone. Never confirm your name or say "yes" to a suspicious caller. Report it to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov. Verify by calling CBP directly at 1-877-CBP-5511, the official number. CBP communicates legitimate matters via USPS mail only, never by Zelle or gift cards.
scams.location: Phone calls to travelers visiting Atlanta or transiting through ATL airport, claiming to be from US Customs/ATL area code (404)
scams.tldr: Callers spoofing Atlanta 404-area-code numbers claim to be US Customs and Border Protection, tell victims a "package containing illegal substances" was seized at ATL airport under their name, and demand $1,000–$5,000 via Zelle, gift cards, or wire transfer to "clear the warrant." CBP never calls travelers demanding payment by phone.

scams.name: MLK Center & Sweet Auburn Tour Touts
scams.description:
The Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park in Sweet Auburn is one of the most visited free heritage sites in the United States. The park covers MLK's birthplace home, Ebenezer Baptist Church, the King Center (with the tomb and reflection pool), and the visitor center, all free and all walk-in except for the birthplace home tour, which requires a free advance reservation. The site's emotional gravity and its status as a "must-see Atlanta experience" make tourists less likely to question a well-presented tout.

Touts outside Ebenezer Baptist Church charge $30 for "private access" or a "guided tour" of a site that has no admission and is fully accessible by simply walking in. Third-party tour operators market "MLK Walking Tour" packages at more than $80 per person for the Sweet Auburn corridor, the same content covered comprehensively and at no cost by the free NPS ranger-led tours departing from the park visitor center. Reserve the free birthplace home tour at recreation.gov, and join the free NPS ranger-led tours at the visitor center. The MLK Center, Ebenezer Baptist Church, and King Center are all free with no booking required, and no paid tour offers access that isn't available to anyone who walks up.
scams.avoidance: Reserve the MLK birthplace home tour at recreation.gov (free). The MLK Center, Ebenezer Baptist Church, and King Center are all free and walk-in. The NPS ranger-led tour is free and higher quality than paid tours. The Sweet Auburn historic district is a free self-guided walk. Skip all paid "MLK walking tours."
scams.location: Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park, Sweet Auburn Historic District, Ebenezer Baptist Church approach, King Center tours
scams.tldr: Street touts outside Ebenezer Baptist Church charge $30 to more than $80 for "private tours" and "guided walking experiences" of a site that is entirely free. The MLK Center, Ebenezer Baptist Church, and King Center are all free walk-ins, and the NPS runs complimentary ranger-led tours superior to any paid offering.

scams.name: Ponce City Market & Beltline Tourist-Menu Overcharge
scams.description:
Ponce City Market, housed in the former Sears, Roebuck building, and the adjacent BeltLine Eastside Trail are central to Atlanta's food and culture scene and worth visiting as experiences. Both also attract tourist-volume pricing: Ponce City Market food stalls run $18–$22 for sandwiches and $10–$14 for casual bites that cost $8–$10 in the neighborhoods immediately to the south. The BeltLine Eastside Trail restaurant strip targets the social-media photo audience, not value-conscious diners.

This is a pricing strategy rather than fraud, but it can catch budget travelers off guard, particularly those who assume Atlanta's lower cost-of-living index extends to its tourist landmarks, which it does not. The gap matters most on multi-day visits, where three meals daily at Ponce City Market and BeltLine prices can cost $30–$50 per person more per day than eating at residential Atlanta prices. Visit Ponce City Market for the atmosphere and eat at mid-tier vendors ($12–$18 per meal), then seek authentic Atlanta food at residential prices in Virginia-Highland, Grant Park, or Cabbagetown. Mary Mac's Tea Room ($18–$28), Busy Bee Cafe ($15–$22), and Paschal's ($22–$35) offer genuine Southern soul food without tourist markup.
scams.avoidance: At Ponce City Market, choose mid-tier vendors such as Holeman and Finch, El Super Pan, and King of Pops ($12–$18). Head to Virginia-Highland or Grant Park for residential-priced Atlanta food. For soul food, try Mary Mac's Tea Room ($18–$28), Paschal's ($22–$35), and Busy Bee Cafe ($15–$22). Avoid the overpriced BeltLine Eastside Trail drink tourism. Check Yelp and Google for Atlanta restaurants with 4.5-plus stars at residential prices.
scams.location: Ponce City Market food hall, Atlanta BeltLine (Eastside Trail) restaurant strips, Buckhead tourist-facing venues
scams.tldr: Ponce City Market food stalls charge more than $20 for sandwiches, and the BeltLine Eastside Trail restaurants charge $14 for cocktails and $18 for small plates. Both are genuine Atlanta destinations, but they are priced 40 to 60 percent above what comparable food costs in the city's residential neighborhoods one mile away.

scams.name: Atlanta Airbnb & Convention-Season Short-Term Rental Fraud
scams.description:
Atlanta hosts annual events that compress hotel inventory to near zero: Dragon Con (late August and early September), Music Midtown (September), Falcons and Hawks home games in fall and winter, the SEC Football Championship (December), and the National Black Arts Festival. The tight market creates a window for fraudulent short-term rental listings to surface at the moment travelers are most anxious about accommodations, willing to pay quickly and less likely to pause and verify.

A Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist listing presents a plausible Midtown or Downtown apartment at 30 to 50 percent below the peak hotel rate, with the discount framed as a "direct booking deal" that requires Zelle, Venmo, or bank transfer to "secure." Multiple victims are charged for the same dates, or the address simply does not exist. On arrival week, the listing is deleted and the host is unreachable; travelers who paid off-platform have no dispute rights with Airbnb, VRBO, or any credit card issuer. Book Atlanta accommodations only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com with platform-protected payment, and for convention weeks book at least three months ahead. Refuse any host request to complete payment outside the booking platform, regardless of the discount offered.
scams.avoidance: Book only through Airbnb, VRBO, or Booking.com with platform-verified payment. Refuse Zelle, Venmo, or bank transfer from "hosts." Verify listings with 20 or more reviews from the last 12 months. Licensed hotels include the Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, Loews, W, and Kimpton Sylvan. Book three or more months ahead for convention weeks to avoid the scam-vulnerable last-minute market.
scams.location: Online — Airbnb listings for Midtown, Downtown, Buckhead during Atlanta convention season (January, March, May, October); Facebook Marketplace short-term rentals
scams.tldr: During Atlanta convention weeks, including Dragon Con, Music Midtown, and the SEC Championship, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist listings advertise Midtown and Downtown apartments at 30 to 50 percent below the going hotel rate and require Zelle or bank transfer payment before arrival. The listing is fraudulent, the address doesn't exist, or multiple victims have paid for the same dates.
